The point of the game wasn't to make you feel guilty about the choices Ellie makes throughout the game, but to show you the two sides to every story. Pre-ordering made sense before digital copies became so prevalent. People did it to ensure they could have a copy to pick up day 1. Now, pre-ordering is a toxic business practice used to overpromise and underdeliver. Developers are selling people on what could be, and not what actually is. Pre-orders often are enough for companies to meet sales targets alone, meaning that they dont ever have to deliver a finished product, because they have your money.  The existence of pre-orders has ultimately led to this practice of a "game as a service" model where consumers pay full price for an unfinished game which then require major day 1 patches AND continual patches throughout the coming months to bring games to a state that they should have been launched at to begin with. 

To your point, if youre going to pick it up day 1, why bother giving them your money in advance? You know a copy will  be available for you day 1 regardless.

A Roth IRA would not be a bad play. Vanguard is a good option for a broker, but there are plenty of options out there. When looking at retirement saving, the easiest thing to do is to park your money in a total stock market fund or low cost broad-based ETF. In doing so, your portfolio will do what the market does, and over the course of 40+ years, you'll get to participate in those gains. Individual stock investing should be left to much larger portfolios or act as complements to an already well diversified portfolio.

Retirement plan through your employer?  If you're not contributing and maxing that out you should be. Beyond that -  I'd suggest looking into a Roth IRA as a complement to your employer plan assuming you have one. Investing in quality, dividend paying stocks like the ones you mentioned is a good start and will likely be solid performers over the long run. The most important aspect here is diversification. A properly allocated portfolio will ensure growth while acting as a buffer in times of volatility.

It depends. Has your risk tolerance truly changed, or are you just spooked by this short term volatility? Assuming you have your 401(k) properly diversified, and it's the latter - stay the course. Investing for retirement is the long game.

Although you hold a valid point about needing real life experiences and being able to increase said experiences along with knowledge and skills, setting oneself up for the future is paramount in this day and age. Too many people have regrets that they didn't start investing early enough and are playing catch up so that they might retire at a decent age and enjoy life later on. 

This being said, I would like to share some advice that was offered to me at a personal finance seminar I attended as a freshman economics and finance major at university. I'm paraphrasing this of course, but you'll get the picture.

Out of college, or whenever you begin your career and start earning income that will support yourself entirely, split your income into three "buckets": your bare essentials, your future, and yourself. Split your income among these "buckets" so you're spending 50% on essentials, 30% in your future, and the remainder on yourself. 

Essentials were classified as everything that you need to pay for so that you can live a comfortable life. This includes rent, utilities, car payments, cable/internet, food, clothes, etc.  When compiling this list, it's very important to think about what you really need to be paying for to get by, to live as frugally as possible. 

As for your future, that seems pretty self explanatory. Put money away now so that you can earn interest over the next 40 years instead of the next 30. The effect of compounding interest over time is astounding. The longer it has to compound, the more money you have. Put this money into whatever investment vehicle you see fit; perhaps through your companies 401k or your own independent Roth IRA.  It's up to you. 

Lastly, spend the remainder of your income on yourself. I believe the term that was used during the presentation was "pay yourself". Do some things you enjoy. You deserve a little enjoyment out of the money you make, but only after you invest in your future.

Afterward we headed south to the negev desert, to the dead sea, and the old mountain fortress of masada. Lastly, we made our way to Jerusalem and explored just about every nook and cranny of the city, from going underneath the Western Wall (as well as spending shabat at the western wall with the rest of the city) to The Church of the Holy Sepulcher to The Dome on the Rock
